title: This Summer-to-Fall Vegetable Dish Is Straight Out of the South of France
summary:
If you’re overwhelmed by the abundance of zucchinis and tomatoes this time of year, make Tian Provençal.

The post This Summer-to-Fall Vegetable Dish Is Straight Out of the South of France appeared first on Wine Enthusiast.
content:
The end of summer is always a little bittersweet. But the cooler weather paired with the last burst of summer produce is a sweet spot worth celebrating. 

Cookbook author and master entertainer Chloe Crane-Leroux’s Tian Provençal makes the most of the season. Similar to ratatouille, but made with a slightly different technique, thinly sliced zucchini, eggplant, and tomatoes are paired with a robust sauce of roasted red peppers, tomatoes, and fresh herbs. It is then baked in the oven until the sauce is bubbly and the vegetables are lightly caramelized—making the most of bright, seasonal flavors without killing your AC bill at the height of peak summer heat.

It’s also downright beautiful, which is why Crane-Leroux loves serving it to guests. It feeds a crowd and seamlessly pairs with a wide variety of starters and sides, and she says, “it is really the perfect transition meal from summer to fall.”

How Chloé Crane-Leroux Sweeps Dinner Guests Away to Provence

If you can’t go all the way to France, hosting a Provençal-style soiree is the next best thing. Here’s how the cookbook author and photographer pulls it off.

Tian Provençal

Courtesy of Chloe Crane-Leroux

Ingredients

2 medium zucchinis, thinly sliced
2 medium eggplants, thinly sliced
3 large ripe tomatoes, thinly sliced
1 medium red onion, roughly chopped
2 garlic cloves, minced
1 red bell pepper
2 tablespoons extra virgin olive oil
1 (14 ounce) can diced tomatoes
1 teaspoon fresh thyme leaves
1 teaspoon fresh rosemary, finely chopped
½ teaspoon sea salt
½ teaspoon freshly ground black pepper
1 handful fresh basil, roughly torn

Directions

Preheat your grill to high. Place the red bell pepper directly on the grill grates. Char it, turning occasionally, until the skin is blackened and blistered, for 8 to 10 minutes.

Remove from the grill, place in a bowl, and cover with a lid or plastic wrap for 10 minutes to steam. Peel off the charred skin, remove the seeds, and roughly chop the flesh.

Preheat your oven to 375°F (190°C). Thinly slice the zucchini, eggplant, and tomatoes into uniform rounds, about ¼ inch thick. Set aside.

Heat the olive oil in a large oven-safe pan or skillet over medium heat. Add the minced garlic and roughly chopped red onion. Sauté for 2 to 3 minutes, stirring occasionally, until the onion is soft and fragrant.

Stir in the canned diced tomatoes, grilled bell pepper, fresh thyme, rosemary, salt, and pepper. Let the mixture simmer for 5 minutes, then spread it evenly across the bottom of the pan.

Arrange the zucchini, eggplant, and tomato slices following the form of your baking dish (mine is round) on top of the tomato-onion base, alternating them to create a colorful pattern. Slightly overlap the slices for a visually appealing presentation.

Drizzle the layered vegetables with a little extra olive oil.

Sprinkle lightly with salt and pepper.

Cover the pan loosely with foil and bake for 30 minutes.

Remove the foil and bake for an additional 20 to 30 minutes, or until the vegetables are tender and slightly caramelized.

Remove from the oven and let it cool. Sprinkle basil and serve.

title: How Chloé Crane-Leroux Sweeps Dinner Guests Away to Provence
summary:
If you can’t go all the way to France, hosting a Provençal-style soiree is the next best thing. Here’s how the cookbook author and photographer pulls it off.

The post How Chloé Crane-Leroux Sweeps Dinner Guests Away to Provence appeared first on Wine Enthusiast.
content:
On her first trip to Provence in 2023, visual artist and cookbook author Chloé Crane-Leroux felt like her heart was “cracked open.” During the trip, she was drawn to the region in a way she had never experienced before. “I was like ‘this is where I’m meant to be,’” she says. “I just felt like I belonged there.” 

Since then, Crane-Leroux has been splitting her time between Provence and New York with trips across the sea at least every two months, but her connection to France didn’t come out of nowhere. Throughout her childhood, she visited Paris and other areas of the countryside with her family nearly every year.

Her passion for cooking and entertaining also stems from her parents, who were avid hosts all throughout her childhood. “We just always wanted to have friends over, and that’s exactly what my parents did,” she says. “They had friends over all the time, and I just really, really loved that.” 

As she grew up and went off on her own, Crane-Leroux continued both of those childhood traditions. She regularly hosted friends for plant-based dinners at her New York City apartment and traveled to France. Next spring, she’s bringing fans along for the journey with her first immersive retreat in the heart of Provence at the Hôtel Crillon le Brave.

Over five days, Crane-Leroux will take attendees into her world with trips to local food and antique markets, an olive oil tasting, and hands-on cooking workshops. In anticipation of the retreat, we caught up with the plant-based host extraordinaire to get her inside tips on throwing an unforgettable Provençal-style party—sans meat. Whether you want to celebrate seasonal produce, save money while serving farmers’ market fare, or just level up your hosting game, read on for Crane-Leroux’s tips on being the consummate host.

Open Up with Apéro

“Hosting doesn’t have to be scary,” Crane-Leroux says. “A lot of people get intimidated because they want it to be perfect and they overthink it.” That’s why she insists that the path to becoming a better host starts with small steps.

“My favorite thing is apéro, which is basically a French happy hour,” she says. All you need are some small bites and drinks, which Crane-Leroux says can last the whole evening or can trickle into a full dinner. “It’s the perfect way to start hosting because it’s not a full meal and it doesn’t feel so extravagant.”

Wine is Crane-Leroux’s beverage pairing of choice, especially when looking for ease. “In the summer, I love a glass of crisp rosé, especially if we’re starting with little bites,” she says. Sometimes, in the fall or winter, she’ll gravitate towards a red wine—”they’re a bit cozier”—but she enjoys whites year round. “You can never go wrong with a Sancerre or a Chablis.”

While she rarely enjoys cocktails, Crane-Leroux will sometimes indulge in a wine spritz. If you’re up to the challenge of making it at home, go for her favorite combo: a Lillet spritz with a wedge of grapefruit.

Showcase Fresh, Seasonal Ingredients

Whether you’re focusing on snacks or a sit-down dinner, Crane-Leroux is all about celebrating the seasons—even when it comes to tablescapes and decor. She incorporates seasonal vegetables into the floral arrangements or goes full-on produce-focused, like this whimsical tomato tablescape. The rest of the table setting builds on this rustic approach with mismatched wine glasses and candlesticks of varying heights. Crane-Leroux says that this “adds this kind of coziness that everybody loves at a dinner.”

Crane-Leroux also considers seasonality and visual presentation while planning her menus.

“Going to the farmers’ market and getting inspired by what is out there is the best way to come up with a recipe,” she says. “Honing into these key ingredients and eating in a way that just feels like how the earth intended is so great.”

Obviously, this changes throughout the year. In summer and early fall when the tomatoes and zucchini are still really good, Crane-Leroux likes to serve Tian Provençal. Similar to ratatouille but with a prettier presentation, the traditional dish spotlights fresh produce and looks absolutely gorgeous on the dinner table.

Read More

Galettes and rustic tarts are another eye-catching way that Crane-Leroux likes to center seasonal produce. They’re endlessly adaptable and deceptively easy, especially considering how impressive they appear.

“Truly, you can put anything on puff pastry, and I think it would be amazing,” she says. In the summertime and early fall, this often manifests as tomato or zucchini galettes, while cooler months lend themselves well to winter squashes.

Wine Picks Should Elevate the Produce

Plant-based food often gets a bad rap for being difficult to pair, but Crane-Leroux insists that couldn’t be farther from the truth.

“Wine comes from the earth and plant-based food comes from the earth,” she says. “The flavors of the wine can be complementary to a specific vegetable,” she says. “So you can really take dishes that have those particular ingredients and tie it back to a certain wine.”

Have you ever tasted a wine that distinctly feels like biting into a tomato? Crane-Leroux has, and she finds that pairing those kinds of wines with a dish featuring farm-fresh heirloom tomatoes beautifully elevates the flavors of each. She also loves pairing an earthy Lambrusco with red sauce pizza or a rich Port with cherry pie.

“A wine that brings those flavors out will also just make the dish even better,” Crane-Leroux says.

Let Guests Handle Dessert—But Add a Signature Touch

When guests inevitably offer to bring something, Crane-Leroux will often concede dessert. 

“It lifts a little bit of weight off of me from cooking,” she says, and it can add a fun element of surprise to the evening if you’re not quite sure what they’re bringing. Even so, she likes to prepare some sort of accompaniment for dessert to add a homemade feeling and an extra special touch. This could take the shape of anything from ice cream or caramel sauce to shaved chocolate or edible flowers to decorate. 

“You didn’t do a full-blown dessert—your guest brought that,” she says, “but then adding that little touch as the host, even just to make the dish prettier, I think that is the best of both worlds.”

title: Why the World’s Top Sommelier Renounced Luxury to Farm Obscure Grapes
summary:
Rajat Parr was one of the most sought-after somms on the planet before he left it all to become a vigneron on California’s Central Coast.

The post Why the World’s Top Sommelier Renounced Luxury to Farm Obscure Grapes appeared first on Wine Enthusiast.
content:
Not long ago, Rajat Parr was living the life of the most sought-after sommelier on the planet. The Calcutta-born, Hyde Park-educated supertaster was jet-setting from San Francisco to Paris, consulting on restaurant openings, writing award-winning books, tasting the best wines ever made, and hanging out with the world’s wealthiest collectors. He was making more money than he knew what to do with, and could have ridden that train all the way to a princely retirement.

But today, Parr looks more like a peasant, dressed in faded overalls and dusty boots, with a beaded wooden necklace around his neck. He spends his days tending to grapevines hours away from any fancy restaurant or big city, feeding hay to sheep and oyster shells to chickens. His work, for which he earns almost no income, is never done. And yet, he’s appreciating every minute.

“This is what I do all day long,” he tells me on a sunny yet cool July afternoon at his vineyard on the San Luis Obispo coast. He’s tying tiny strings around bunches of Gringet vines, a task he’ll repeat on this ancient grape variety from France’s Savoie region and then on his Trousseau vines, which hail from the Jura, about 5,000 times. “That’s my job for the next month.”

It’s been nine years since Parr started operating Phelan Farm in San Simeon, and three years since he added Stolo Vineyards—and its winery and tasting room—in nearby Cambria to the Parr Wines portfolio. (Both will be called Phelan Farm starting this vintage.) After grafting over much of each property to obscure varieties and shifting from mostly conventional farming to strictly organic and dry, the struggle has been very real.

The vines were shocked by the dramatic shift in techniques, and the ensuing seasons further decimated harvests. Then the global thirst for wine started to dry up, putting the whole project on the brink of financial ruin. Though Parr is all but worshipped by the wine industry, many fellow winemakers in recent years have wondered quietly what the hell he was doing—risking so much on extreme viticulture, making somewhat weird, sometimes unappealing natural wines, living like a hermit in the sleepy, creepily quiet Cambria hills.

With his typical grace, Parr acknowledges these outside impressions and even admits that some of his early vintages weren’t so “stable.” But he’s convinced that his theories and efforts are finally starting to pay off, and he can’t help but smile while looking at his 2026 crop.

“I just feel happy looking at this,” he says. “This year is a bigger crop than the past four years put together.”

Middle Pathing

It’s easy to compare Parr’s journey with the Buddha’s path to enlightenment. Both hail from India and both renounced lives of luxury to seek a more meaningful existence, embracing asceticism over excess. It doesn’t hurt that Parr is cherubic in demeanor, ponderous in thought like a wise monk, and refers to finding “the Middle Path” quite often.

Few people know his journey as intimately as the writer Jordan Mackay. He met Parr while reporting an article on San Francisco somms almost 25 years ago and later co-authored Secrets of the Sommeliers and The Sommelier’s Atlas of Taste with him. Mackay felt it was “profound” when Parr started making his own wine, initially with the late Jim Clendenen of Au Bon Climat in the Santa Maria Valley.

“There was a lot to lose by putting himself in the winemaking world after ascending to the top of the somm world,” said Mackay, noting that Parr was one of the first prominent somms to do so. “I love that Raj was unafraid.”

Parr shifted from celebrating the world’s iconic traditional wines to embracing the natural wine movement around 2018. “It was a strange thing for a person who spent so much time in Burgundy with the very wealthiest wine collectors,” said Mackay. “It seemed like almost overnight he renounced all that and started dressing differently and hanging with the wine world’s version of hippies.”

Parr’s decision to make Phelan Farm his full-time pursuit was triggered by a confluence of conditions. His 2018 book tour left him exhausted, and an ayahuasca experience the following year got him thinking about the future. He worried that his partnership with the Santa Barbara brands Sandhi and Domaine de la Côte—which top wine critics hailed as the world’s best Pinot Noir in the documentary Somm 3—was on the rocks. (Parr was right: He was eventually cut out of that business, taking away nothing, in 2025.)

Then came the pandemic, which knocked the restaurant industry to its knees. He voluntarily resigned from his job at the Michael Mina’s lucrative restaurant group, moved permanently from Santa Barbara to Cambria, and went all in on Phelan Farm. Had the pandemic not happened? “I would have continued my life,” said Parr.

Instead, he became a true vigneron, toiling in the vines every day, working solo in the cellar. “I’d never farmed anything. I’d never ridden a tractor,” laughed Parr, who spent the first three months reading every book about vineyard management he could find. “For two years, I didn’t see anybody. I never imagined I’d be working in a vineyard like this.”

From the Alps to the Pacific

Parr is fascinated with growing grapes most American winemakers don’t even know about, and it’s not merely a nonconformist quest, as many assume. Rather, he studied the growing season in Cambria, where the fog-swamped, wind-cooled weather rarely gets above 80 degrees until the last week of August. That leaves a very tight window for grapes to mature by their October harvest.

“What varieties would ripen in that window?” pondered Parr. “All of these varieties are Alpine.” By that, he means the Jura and Savoie regions near the Alps in southeastern France, where, just like Cambria, the soils are laden with clay. Double bonus.

His theory is finally starting to play out this year: Savagnin, Trousseau, Gringet, Jacquère, Mondeuse, Pink Chardonnay, and other varieties are all showing solid crops. Not every grape worked, though. “I have Altesse planted that just doesn’t grow, and Poulsard can be challenging,” he said.

Of course, how to farm was more important to Parr than what to farm. All of his “hero producers” are organic dry farmers, so that’s what he committed to at Phelan Farm, where the 33 combined acres of vineyards had always been farmed conventionally. Parr dropped the pesticides cold turkey, turned off the irrigation, and experimented with all sorts of regenerative techniques. The vines—including the older plantings of Pinot Noir, Chardonnay, and Syrah—were traumatized, nearly to death.

“I made so many mistakes in the vineyard,” said Parr, who’s now watching the soil go from compacted to fluffy, and the grapes slowly adjust to dry farming. “Unless you do it and you fail, you’re never going to know your limits. What I know today is how resilient nature is, and how to bring it back.”

The Gentle Hand

In recent years, Parr grew his team to include his girlfriend, Amanda Carpenter, who does a bit of everything; husband-and-wife viticulturist Daniel Callan and winemaker Anna Callan-Paredes; dry-farming consultant Dylan Grigg from Australia; and general manager Scott Wills, who had been at Stolo Vineyards before Parr took over.

“He’s so gentle, but also methodical in his thinking,” said Wills. “This is the guy you want as your boss.”

Together, they produce a dizzying range of wines under numerous Parr Wines brands. But going forward, he’ll primarily focus on Phelan Farm and Brij, a larger-production, négociant label for San Luis Obispo Coast Pinot Noir and Chardonnay.

They’re all learning about these ancient but new-to-California varieties in real time. There’s the Gringet (“a little like Chenin, a little like Grüner,” said Parr), the Pink Chardonnay (“oh, no one does it,” he said when asked how it was made in Europe), and the flagship Autrement red blend of Pinot Noir, Gamay, and Mondeuse (“this is our postcard of Cambria”).

The most promising may be Savagnin, which has a late bud break, ripens late, and is somewhat mildew resistant. “I think this is the future white grape of climate change, everywhere,” said Parr. “Maybe in 10 to 20 years or so, even Burgundy will plant this variety since Chardonnay is getting harder and harder.”

Whether the rest of the world realizes this is Parr’s big gamble. Because of the vineyard struggles, declining visitation, and a generally down wine market, Parr nearly lost everything last year. But he doesn’t regret the way he’s done it. “I have to do it right until I can’t,” he said.

His original mission remains pure. “I want to plant a vineyard that is going to outlive everybody,” Parr said. “I want to make simple, delicious wines.”

content:
Come Together, Right Now, Over Me

Live events are helping us heal.

I’m coming off a pretty great four-month run of live events. I’ve been lucky enough to attend both Phillies and Yankees games this summer, a 25-year anniversary tour for Jimmy Eat World, the World Cup Final, the Eagles season opener (go Birds!) and, possibly best of all, Robyn at Barclays Center. 

I’m not telling you this to brag, although I do admit it’s an enviable list. I’m telling you this because of the herculean effort it took for a mother of two young children to attend that many live events in a short span of time. It clearly shows that attending these large-scale experiences has become a newfound priority in my life. 

And I’m not the only one. Live Nation events hosted a record 159 million fans in 2025, and 2026 ticket sales were already running double digits ahead early this year. By Q2, nearly 49 million people attended its shows in just the quarter, up 10%. Eventbrite found 79% of 18-to-35-year-olds planned to attend more events in 2026, describing the trend as a “Reset to Real.”

We’re not new to the value of gathering in the wine world. But there’s something to be gained from its newfound explosion in popularity. We’re all looking to feel … something. That something comes from interacting with other people—not our phones.

We all know the dopamine rise and crash from the unfettered access to social media. Like the empty calories after a batch of disappointingly soggy French fries, virtual rage bait continues to drag us in, divide us, and burn us out on everything from politics to how to properly fold socks. 

And yet, it seems as though we’re increasingly all coming to the same realization: there’s got to be more to life than getting worked up by a screen. That’s where live events have found their footing. They force us to take a pause, take in the real world, and experience human connection. 

Maybe what we’re craving isn’t just in-person events. Maybe we’re craving presence. Live music, sports, food, and wine all have something in common: they ask us to pay attention IRL. 

Wine is certainly worthy of deep attention, but for the industry to grow, it needs to accept that it need not be the focal point of every occasion. Just being invited to the party is a win.

That’s something Beatbox figured out early on. Their laser focus on music festivals earned them a near half a billion dollar valuation. Our friends at Jackson Family Wine’s Kendall Jackson’s partnership with the NBA and La Crema’s with the WNBA showed us that wine’s place in basketball is solid. Gallo’s Barefoot partnership with the NFL put wine at the kickoff of America’s favorite pastime. And T. Edwards’ Gulp Hablo’s partnership with Bowery Presents shows that millennial hipsters can—and do—have fun with wine too. All of these brands have figured out how to work their way into this next big wave of cultural touchpoints. Having wine available at live events frankly helps the entire industry at large. 

I can tell you that at most of the events I attended this summer, I had a glass of wine at some point in the evening. Maybe it was the glass of cold Albariño at dinner with friends before the show. Or perhaps it was a can of Prisma Sauvignon Blanc in an arena howling the lyrics to “Dancing on My Own” while (ironically) dancing alongside thousands of other fans. Maybe it’s the natty orange wine in the Brooklyn bar afterwards, when the effervescent pleasure of the night is just too high to go home. Wine was there. I didn’t talk about the tasting notes, the score, or the winemaker’s story. But it was still a huge part of the night. 

Wine doesn’t need to be the main event, or the headliner, but it does need to be there. 

Bringing wine to these real-world experiences reinforces its place in our rekindled love affair with real life. That means we, as an industry, have earned a part of the moment, the memory, and the occasions that are a core component of what it means to be alive. We just need to make sure wine continues to get the invite. 

Jacqueline Strum

President & Publisher of Wine Enthusiast Media

title: This Punchy Espresso Cocktail Has Afro-Caribbean Flair
summary:
Cafecito de La Mesa, which translates to “a little coffee at the table,” is an aromatic brandy cocktail from chef Nelson German.

The post This Punchy Espresso Cocktail Has Afro-Caribbean Flair appeared first on Wine Enthusiast.
content:
Nelson German understands how flavors work. He’s the chef-owner of alaMar Dominican Kitchen and the Afro-Latin cocktail lounge Sobre Mesa in Oakland, California, and was a contestant on Top Chef Season 18.

Yet, when he began writing his new book, Caribbean Cocktails, which centers German’s exploration of the Spanish-speaking African diaspora, he realized the flavors he grew up with—plantains, braised meats, rich spice blends—weren’t just Dominican; they were African, too. Further, he found the cocktail world underutilizes ingredients and stories tied to the African diaspora, like coffee.

“Coffee’s origins trace back to Ethiopia, where popular lore tells of Kaldi, a herder whose goats danced after eating coffee berries,” he says. The French brought coffee to Martinique in 1720, and from there it spread across the Caribbean, to Haiti, Jamaica, and the Dominican Republic.

It’s also a key flavor in the Cafecito de la Mesa cocktail, which translates to “a little coffee at the table,” and ties into German’s childhood memories.

“Sitting with my mom after family dinners, sipping rich, comforting Café Bustelo and talking about school and life are my fondest memories from growing up,” he recalls. Today, he’s more likely to enjoy coffee from a local roaster in Oakland. “This cocktail, like my coffee rituals, is a reflection of both tradition and evolution.”

Here, the warmth of brandy blends with nutty coconut and cinnamon spice, plus a hint of orange blossom from Amaro Montenegro, a bittersweet Italian liqueur. The punchy strength of espresso echoes “the Dominican love of bold coffee flavors,” German says.

Cafecito de la Mesa

From Caribbean Cocktails: Drinks and Bites from the Afro-Latino Diaspora, by Nelson German and Andréa Lawson Gray (Ten Speed Press, 2026)

Ingredients

1 ½ ounces brandy
½ ounce Amaro Montenegro
½ ounce coconut cream
½ ounce Demerara syrup*
¼ teaspoon ground cinnamon
2 dashes chicory pecan bitters
1 ounce espresso, brewed
Burnt orange peel, for garnish**

Directions

In a mixing glass, combine all ingredients (no ice). Stir to combine, then pour over a large ice cube in a rocks glass.

*To make Demerara syrup: In a small saucepan over low heat, combine ½ cup Demerara sugar and ½ cup water. Stir gently until the sugar has fully dissolved and the syrup is clear, 3–5 minutes. Remove from heat and cool to room temperature. Transfer to a glass container. Keeps refrigerated for up to 1 month.

**To make the burnt orange peel garnish: Cut a wide strip of orange peel, avoiding the pith. Briefly pass the peel over an open flame until lightly charred and aromatic.

Hold the citrus peel over the drink and quickly twist it to release the aromatic oils over the surface of the drink. Run the peel around the rim of the glass, then use the peel to garnish the drink.

title: The Best Wines to Serve at a Wedding, According to Industry Pros
summary:
When it comes to wedding wine, somms and beverage directors know best. Here’s their advice, from what to pour and why.

The post The Best Wines to Serve at a Wedding, According to Industry Pros appeared first on Wine Enthusiast.
content:
Wine has a way of fueling weddings. Its roles may include, but are not limited to: Champagne toasts to the happy couple, glasses that enliven the dance floor, and pours that buffer interactions with quirky relatives and old flames.

While grocery store bottles will certainly be on budget for all of the above, sommeliers (and picky family members) will argue that weddings are special, so it’s not the time to opt for ordinary or everyday wines. 

“It’ssuch a thoughtful touch to avoid the same old Prosecco and grocery store brands people are accustomed to,” says Katy Kindred, founder of Kindred Hospitality restaurant group, which often hosts outdoor and indoor weddings. “Most guests don’t notice when it’s a standard wine, but when your wine is thoughtfully considered, you notice.”

We’re not suggesting you throw out the budget in favor of old vintages and the best of Burgundy. “You want the big day to be special,” Kindred says. “It’s not just a party: it’s the first day of a marriage. But you also want to start off your marriage right by being a good steward of your resources.”

To take the guesswork out of your wedding wine, sommeliers and event experts weigh in on how to pick the perfect big-day bottles.

How to Choose Wine for Weddings

Bryce Faucheaux, general manager of Louisiana’s Old Metairie Bottle Shop, and Missy Auge, wine director at Santa Fe’s Bishop’s Lodge, Auberge Resorts Collection, follow a few rules when selecting bottles for events or weddings.

  • Consider what’s popular. Don’t stick to your own preferences. “Anticipate what people might ask for,” Faucheaux says. “Sauvignon Blanc or a Cabernet Sauvignon–based blend are almost always requested.” Stock accordingly.
  • Order exuberantly. A general rule of thumb is one bottle per person. That may seem like overkill, but it’s better to be left with extras than run dry during dinner.
  • Look locally. “Talk with local wine shops,” Faucheaux says. “They might be able to work with you and negotiate a better price for bulk orders.” Another option? Inquire within nearby wineries—they also may be willing to offer a better price on large orders (added plus: you’re shopping local).
  • Fit the wine to the weather, not just the occasion. “My brother got married in August in New Orleans,” Faucheaux says. “So, I picked some refreshing styles of white wine, as well as a chillable red.” At a winter wedding? You can probably hold off on the pét-nat.
  • Be mindful of the food. “If the wedding is going to focus on seafood, then oaky dark-fruited Napa Valley Cabernet Sauvignon is probably not the best option,” Faucheaux says. “Loire Valley whites and reds are very easy to work with. Refreshing, mineral-driven styles of Chenin Blanc from Vouvray are always a nice option. As far as reds, Cabernet Franc from Chinon can be very refreshing.”
  • Keep it approachable. “You don’t want to serve really crazy, expensive wine that no one will appreciate or understand, nor do you want to serve wine so obscure that your guests will be afraid of it,” Auge says.
  • And don’t fuss too much: “Choose one white and one red to pass around for dinner, and don’t over-think the pairing too much,” says Auge. “This is a party, not a wine pairing dinner. Just pick something that is easy and tasty to drink on its own.”
  • Split the selection. “Have a few special wines off to the side for the bride and groom,” Faucheaux says. There’s no better time to break open that vintage Champagne or baller Burgundy—the guests will understand. “It is their day, after all, so make sure that they have a couple of their favorite styles,” he adds. “And if you can, save a few bottles for future anniversaries.”
  • Bubbles are for every occasion. “Champagne has gotten very expensive,” says Faucheaux. “So, Prosecco is usually my go-to bubble for large crowds, but there are many extremely well-made examples beyond Champagne.” Cava, Corpinnat, and Crémant are great options for large events.
  • DIY labels: If you don’t care about guests name-checking the bottles, consider customizing your own labels (with your initials or a sentimental illustration) and adhering them to the bottles.

The Best Wines for a Wedding

Surefire Crowd Pleasers

Matthew Jacobson, head sommelier at Vancouver’s Fairmont Pacific Rim, recommends keeping things simple at large events. “I try not to lean too far into the esoteric,” he says. “Don’t go too sweet, too spicy, or too acidic. Try to stick to tried and true styles, made in traditional ways.”

For whites, Jacobson recommends the following crowd-pleasers: Chablis, Sancerre, and Pinot Grigio. For reds, he opts for Etna Rosso for a Pinot-adjacent budget pick, but also enjoys classics like Nebbiolo, Chianti, Bordeaux, and California Cabs. 

Wine Enthusiast recommends:

Cantina Terlano 2024 Tradition Pinot Bianco Pinot Bianco (Alto Adige)

Baked apples and fresh pears mingling with lemon curd like a pastry chef’s morning prep, everything rich but precisely measured. The palate keeps that balance between power and grace, candied citrus and warm bread notes flowing with the confidence of a winery that’s been mastering this dance since forever. Editors’ Choice. 93 Points — Jeff Porter

$24 Wine.come

CheckMate 2022 Fool’s Mate Chardonnay (Okanagan Valley)

Kick back and enjoy these orchard aromas of nectarines and yellow apples, not to mention wisps of toasted filberts and chamomile flowers. The wine’s modest acidity combines with a creamy texture and a bit of body to create a sinfully smooth sipping experience. The flavors of key lime pie, shortbread and lemon verbena tea are equally decadent. 92 Points — Michael Alberty

$87 Saratoga Wine

Tenuta delle Terre Nere 2024 Etna DOC Rosso Nerello Mascalese (Etna Rosso)

A cool, fresh nose offers aromas of blackberries, black plums, pepper and earth. Flavors of sweet blackberry jam and warm citrus headline the palate, before a dark chocolate ganache element takes over on the finish, lifted by flakes of salt but also reined in by tannins. 95 Points — Danielle Callegari

$31 Wine.com

Champagne

If you have a budget for higher-end bubbles, Auge recommends the gold standard. “I firmly believe that an occasion as important as a wedding deserves real Champagne,” she says.

And while larger Champagne houses have name recognition that can impress guests, Wine Enthusiast Writer-at-Large Aleks Zecevic would opt for “grower” bottles, a type of Champagne in which the winemakers grow their own grapes.

Wine Enthusiast recommends:

Louis Roederer 2018 Starck Brut Nature Blanc Champagne Blend (Champagne)

This expression embodies grace, with aromas of fresh pear, white peach, jasmine and violet framed by a subtle vein of pulverized seashell and chalk. The palate is guided by mouthwatering acidity and fine mousse, carrying citrus oils and crushed stone with quiet precision into a long, elegant finish. Proper aeration allows the mineral edges to open fully, delivering an irresistible and finely tuned sip. Editors’ Choice. 95 Points — Anna-Christina Cabrales

$110 Millesima

Krug NV Grande Cuvée 173ème Édition Brut Champagne Blend (Champagne)

The nose is immediately inviting, filled with toasted brioche topped with baked apple, pear and citrus peel, soft florals and spice for depth. The palate is generous and finely textured, balancing bright acidity with a creamy mousse that carries lemon confit, honeyed stone fruit enveloped in a nutty pastry. It finishes long, saline and utterly compelling, leaving a lasting impression of finesse and energy. Editors’ Choice. 96 Points — A.C.C.

$272 Wine.com

Charles Heidsieck NV Champagne Charlie Cellared in 2020 Champagne Blend (Champagne)

Captivating aromas of white peach and green apple unfold into wildflowers, light toffee, macadamia and a delicate mineral vein. The palate is precise, with poised orchard fruit that gains weight and intensity with aeration. A subtle toasty layer emerges adding depth, while bright acidity carries a long, chalky finish. Approachable with a brief decant, yet built to age. Ideal alongside butter-poached lobster to showcase its richness. Cellar Selection. 98 Points — A.C.C.

$580 Keg N Bottle

Italian Bubbles

If you’re set on serving bubbly but are worried about budget, Italian bubbles may be your new best friend. WE Writer-at-Large Jeff Porter says they are the perfect tool for navigating that price-quality balance.

“I feel that metodo classico wines offer great value and quality,” he says. “From Italy, you can find Franciacorta, Alta Langa, or Trento DOC. All three are great wines made like Champagne but not as expensive.”

Wine Enthusiast recommends:

Ca’ del Bosco MV Cuvée Prestige 48 Edizione Extra Brut Sparkling Blend (Franciacorta)

This is the calling card and it earns that title with every sip. Baked bread, roasted pear, warmed honey and toasted nuts layered over a core of real depth and energy that sets the stage and raises the bar in the same breath. Full bodied and built to last, it moves with the ease and authority of something that has been done many times and perfected along the way. Close your eyes and you are already somewhere far more interesting than here. 94 Points — J.P.

$38 Zachys

Ettore Germano 2017 pas dosè Blanc de Blanc Chardonnay (Alta Langa)

This wine took eight years to arrive and carries every one of them with complete assurance. It opens like a Hollywood starlet on the red carpet, poised and dressed to kill, baked apples, lemon curd, fresh bread and pressed yellow and white flowers commanding the room with effortless authority. The palate is equally composed, a creamy rounded texture balanced by bright acidity while lemon cream, roasted almond and a long salty finish ensure the exit is just as memorable as the entrance. Drink now through 2035. Cellar Selection. 96 Points — J.P.

$90 Vintage Wine Merchants

Ferrari 2015 Lunelli Riserva Extra Brut Chardonnay (Trento)

Ground ginger and wildflowers swirl around warm, baking apples, creating a nose that’s both cozy and fresh. A pop of zippy lemon follows, with a punchy hit of tart lemon curd adding a crisp edge. This wine plays between warmth and zing, keeping each sip lively and irresistibly drinkable, yet time in the cellar will do magic. Drink Now – 2040. Cellar Selection. 98 Points — J.P.

$100 Wine Express

Albariño 

Albariño is “light, crispy, damn good, and most importantly, you can drink it all night long without getting bored,” says John Burns Paterson, who oversees the Nashville outpost of the NYC stalwart, Frankies Spuntino. “To me, that’s the key to a good wedding wine. Not to mention, it’ll pair with just about any setting.”

Beyond Albariño, Paterson keeps his options simple: one sparkling, one white, and one red. “There is no need to overcomplicate,” he adds. “At the end of the day, the guests just want to celebrate and have a good time.”

Wine Enthusiast recommends:

Mar de Frades 2023 Albariño Albariño (Rías Baixas)

Enticing aromas of grapefruit rind and orange blossom give way to subtle hints of green pepper and white flowers. A pleasing saline character runs throughout, though the finish leans a touch too astringent, leaving the balance ever so slightly askew. 90 Points — Brandon Borcoman

$23 Harrison Wine Vault

Klinker Brick Winery 2024 Albariño (Mokelumne River)

This wine is another excellent example of aromatic white wine produced in an under-the-radar region. If you are an Albarino lover, this wine should be in your glass. It is fresh and zesty with aromas of green papaya, kiwi, and citrus, and notes of sweet basil leaves and vetiver on the nose; the flavors on the palate are high energy, Persian lime, White grapefruit, layered with White pepper, sedimentary rock, and a supple dry finish. pair with fried smelts. Best Buy. 93 Points — Tonya Pitts

$13 Empire Wine

Pinot Blanc

“Pinot Blanc is an easy-drinking, refreshing dry wine with a great balance of ripeness and freshness,” says Faucheaux. “It’s a great alternative to Pinot Grigio, which is fairly familiar to everyone.”

He recommends looking for bottles of Blanc from Alsace, France, in particular. “Some wines can be polarizing for people—too floral, too sweet, too savory or herbaceous,” he says. “But this wine is easy and versatile, subtle and elegant, and it’s honestly a crowd pleaser.”

Wine Enthusiast recommends:

Trimbach 2023 Pinot Blanc Pinot Blanc (Alsace)

Classic and cleanly expressed, showing a crisp mix of apple and Meyer lemon with subtle floral accents. The palate is fresh and well balanced, supported by bright acidity that keeps the wine lively. Straightforward yet polished, finishing with good clarity and poise. 89 Points — Aleks Zecevic

$14 Empire Wines

Castel Sallegg 2023 Leopoldine Pinot Blanc (Alto Adige)

This captures that perfect moment when seasons collide. Magnolia blooms and preserved peaches bask in late summer warmth until mountain herbs and bright citrus announce change is coming. The palate masters the same balancing act, luxurious texture finding harmony with vibrant acidity. A wine that shows how contrast creates beauty. Drink Now – 2045 Editors’ Choice. 95 Points — J.P.

$26 Castel Sallegg

J. Lohr Vineyards & Wines 2023 F&G Vineyard Pinot Blanc (Arroyo Seco)

Pinot Blanc remains a rare standalone grape in California, and this bottling calls that infrequent starring role into question. Rounded aromas of melon, mint and chalk lead from the nose into a firmly structured palate exuberant in apple, pear and lime flavors. Refreshing but with ample body. Editors’ Choice. 91 Points — Matt Kettmann

Inquire with the winery

Verdicchio

Kindred is keen on Verdicchio, a crisp white from the Marche region of Italy. “[Verdicchio is] so delicious and shockingly inexpensive for the quality,” she says. “It’s clean, bright, with a little salinity (thanks to the proximity to the Adriatic Sea) that makes it both refreshing and a bit textured.”

Wine Enthusiast recommends:

Bucci 2021 Villa Bucci Riserva Verdicchio (Verdicchio dei Castelli di Jesi Classico)

Here’s why Italian white wine deserves your cellar’s best real estate: green apple skin and Asian pear meet Meyer lemon with the kind of precision that defines greatness. Fresh herbs and stone notes build a framework for complexity that keeps revealing itself, sip after sip. The palate delivers profound depth without showing off, this is white wine operating at its highest level, as compelling now with dover sole as it will be in 2045 and beyond. Cellar Selection. 97 Points — J.P.

$110 Flatiron Wines & Spirits

Umani Ronchi 2022 Vecchie Vigne Verdicchio (Verdicchio dei Castelli di Jesi Classico Superiore)

A faint, zesty lift of fresh citrus oil sets the stage for an explosion of orchard fruits, crisp Macintosh apples and sweet Seckel pears. The flavors come alive with preserved lemon and a salty, mineral edge, like licking a rock. Tart, electric acidity keeps it zippy and refreshing, making this Verdicchio both lively and energetic. 94 Points — J.P.

title: This French Region Is Making World-Class Pinot Without the Burgundy Price Tags
summary:
For the past several decades, Alsace has been defined by its white wines. Pinot Noir might change that.

The post This French Region Is Making World-Class Pinot Without the Burgundy Price Tags appeared first on Wine Enthusiast.
content:
With its tall bottles and aromatic whites, Alsace wine has been easy to pigeonhole. An outlier in France, often feeling closer in structure to Germany than to its home country, the region is known for winemaking that combines German precision with French finesse. And for the past several decades, at least, Alsace has been defined by its white wines, while reds remained a sidebar.

But something has shifted, under the radar. Without the marketing muscle of Burgundy or the rising buzz of German Spätburgunder, Pinot Noir in Alsace has gotten not just better, but serious. In fact, certain bottles would make you recalibrate what you thought you knew about the region.

“The quality of Alsatian Pinot Noir has been improving for 30 years, with a clear acceleration in the last decade,” says Maxime Barmès of Domaine Barmès-Buecher.

The easy explanation is climate change. Warmer vintages, better ripening, and more color and structure have impacted the wines’ character. But talk to growers, and that narrative starts to unravel. “Global warming can help ripening,” Barmès says, “but in very sunny years, it can also reduce aromatic finesse.”

Foulques Aulagnon, export marketing manager of CIVA (Alsace Wine Board), is more direct: “It is a revival, not an evolution.”

The Long, Twisty History of Alsatian Pinot Noir

Pinot Noir isn’t new to Alsace. During the Holy Roman Empire, the region built its reputation for red wines made from grapes grown in limestone, granite, and marl soils. That history was disrupted by the Thirty Years’ War, after which Alsace was repopulated under Louis XIII and XIV.

“These new farmer families came from Switzerland, Austria, and Germany, and had no tradition of producing serious red wine,” says Aulagnon.

What followed was a long decline. Under the German Empire, Alsace became a source of inexpensive wine. Pinot Noir was pushed to high yields, so the wines lost concentration and were reduced to something thin and simple. By the 1970s, the variety was barely relevant.

Then, came the revival. 

It didn’t begin in the vineyard, but in the classroom. In the 1970s, a new generation of Alsatian winemakers started looking toward Dijon’s Université de Bourgogne rather than Geisenheim’s Hochschule Geisenheim University. Burgundy became the reference point.

“Figures like Pierre Trimbach and René Muré brought back not just techniques, but a different philosophy: lower yields, élevage in oak, longer macerations, site expression,” says Aulagnon.

At estates like Domaine Albert Mann, this shift was decisive. In 1962, Pinot Noir accounted for just 1% of Alsace’s vineyard. Throughout the ‘60s and ‘70s, however, the Barthelmé family (who runs the domaine) began planting it on their best sites, including Hengst and Pfersigberg, and rethinking it entirely.

“Before climate change, there was a change of vision,” says Antoine Barthelmé. “We stopped treating Pinot Noir like a white wine.”

By the late 1980s, terroir-driven Pinot Noir had been reintroduced in Alsace. A second wave followed, with winemakers like Mélanie Pfister and Felix Meyer traveling beyond Burgundy, absorbing global ideas, and refining them back home.

The New Way

In the vineyard, the changes have been just as important. Instead of relying on high-yielding clones, many growers have shifted toward massal selection.

“It’s the mixture that contributes to the complexity in a plot, not a single phenotype,” says Barmès.

These selections tend to produce smaller berries, looser clusters, and more concentration, while diversifying vineyard plantings.

Viticulture has evolved, too. Lower yields are now the norm, often in the range of 30 to 35 hectoliters per hectare. Organic and biodynamic farming has become increasingly central. “Biodynamics naturally regulates yields, brings more depth, and improves the texture of Pinot Noir,” says Barthelmé.

Where Pinot Noir works best in Alsace is still an open question. Clay and marl bring structure and intensity to the wines, while those made in grapes grown in granite lean toward freshness.

“Pinot Noir can express itself on all types of Alsatian soils, as long as the work is done well,” Barmès says.

Barthelmé is more definitive. “There is no debate,” he says. “The matrix of Pinot Noir is limestone.”

In Pursuit of Precision

In the cellar, the shift has been toward restraint. Extraction is gentler, and oak is used more carefully. At some estates, like Barmès-Buecher, Pinot Noir is fully destemmed, with light punch-downs and aging in older barrels. The goal is precision, “to preserve the finesse of the Pinot Noir,” says Barmès.

At other estates, like Albert Mann, the approach is more flexible. Whole cluster fermentation can range from zero to 50 percent or more, while new oak is used sparingly. Barthelmé describes it as an “infusion mindset,” where the role of the winemaker is less to impose than to guide.

A growing number of winemakers are also pursuing a natural style. Christoph Binner and Catherine Riss show how minimal intervention can allow the grape to shine. The result is not a single expression, but a category in motion: Alsace Pinot Noir can be lifted and perfumed or deeper and more structured, depending on site and approach. What unites the best examples is balance.

Alsace is still often compared to Burgundy, if only because consumers need a reference point. But the gap is narrowing. “If you blind taste a great Alsace Pinot and a great Burgundy, Alsace has a good chance of competing with wines ten times more expensive,” says Barmès.

Barthelmé is less interested in comparison. “The future is not about creating a new style, but about being more precise.”

Pinot Noir now accounts for roughly 13% of Alsace’s plantings, up from just 8% in 2008. The growth is steady but measured, with increasing focus on the right sites.

For a region long defined by its whites, that might be the most telling sign of all. Alsace is refining something that was long underestimated.

Bottles to Try

Domaine Muré 2023 Clos Saint Landelin Pinot Noir (Alsace)

Classic and refined, showing a beautifully composed mix of cherry, violet, light licorice root, and subtle sandalwood. The palate is ripe and poised, medium to full in body yet never heavy, with polished tannins and well-integrated acidity providing lift. Elegant, balanced, and quietly powerful, it unfurls with grace into a long, harmonious finish. 93 Points — A.Z.

$63 Domaine Muré

Domaine Sipp-Mack 2023 Pinot Noir Vieilles Vignes Pinot Noir (Alsace)

Very pure and finely detailed, offering a beautiful aromatic mix of rosehip, hibiscus tea, and subtle rooibos. The palate is poised and graceful, with tannins that provide structure yet settle gently, never intruding on the fruit. Balanced and precise, this is a beautifully made Pinot Noir that combines delicacy with quiet depth and polish. Best Buy. 92 Points — A.Z.

$18 Boutique Vini

Trimbach 2023 Réserve Pinot Noir (Alsace)

Pure and finely detailed, showing violet, pomegranate, and rose with admirable clarity. The palate is supple and precise, with melting tannins that provide gentle support before fading seamlessly away. Fresh acidity keeps everything lifted, leaving a mouthwatering, elegant finish that underscores the wine’s poise and balance. 91 Points — A.Z.

title: Why Is It So Hard to Find Filipino Wine in the Philippines?
summary:
The Philippines has some of the best-tasting fruit in the world. So why is local wine so hard to come by?

The post Why Is It So Hard to Find Filipino Wine in the Philippines? appeared first on Wine Enthusiast.
content:
How hard can it be to find Filipino wine in the Philippines? Turns out, the task isn’t as straightforward as it sounds.

Picture the world’s renowned wine-producing regions. Your first thought likely isn’t this Southeast Asian nation made up of thousands of islands. But there’s an inherent natural abundance in the Philippines, a country of mountains, coasts, volcanoes, and jungles. A plethora of fruits—calamansi, banana, mango, pineapple—thrive in its tropical climate. For centuries, produce here has been fermented into tasty beverages, such as basi, a fermented sugarcane wine, and tapuey, a rice wine, to which some Filipinos remain deeply attached.

Local companies like Proudly Promdi are leading the charge in rebranding and popularizing regional drinks as a source of pride. However, even with increased demand, these bottles can be difficult to track down.

Ahead of my 14-hour flight from Seattle to Manila, I drooled over Instagram posts featuring creative cocktails like the Basi Spritz and the Tapuey Negroni. As a first-time visitor to the Philippines, I wanted to sample drinks that I couldn’t make at home.

Proudly Promdi’s tagline touts that they are “rediscovering and celebrating Filipino heritage through artisanal spirits.” Promdi is slang for “from the province,” referring to the rural areas outside Manila, the bustling capital city home to around two million people. While it’s often used as a derogatory term, Proudly Promdi founder Ken Alonso, 39, is reclaiming the word—and the nation’s local wines and spirits.

Take tapuey. It’s made out of glutinous rice, a regional crop. Alonso explained that different varieties, including black, red, white, and brown, each produce their own distinctive taste. “Since we’re an archipelagic country, and we’re so scattered, each region or island will also have different interpretations of a different Filipino spirit,” he told me.

“We use a lot of tropical ingredients,” he said. “We in the Philippines arguably have the best-tasting fruits in the world: the sweetest ones, the juiciest ones.”

Unlike traditional dry grape wines, the fruit wines (which people also refer to as spirits) lean on the sweeter side, Alonso said. Sugar supports the fermentation process, as “these are fermented spirits only and not distilled spirits,” he added. “That’s actually very unique.”

On the morning of the Lunar New Year in February, I was on the hunt for Filipino wine and sunscreen. A local directed my fiancé and me down the Taytay-El Nido National Highway to a convenience store crowded with early birds in the figurative sense (shoppers) and the literal sense (chickens).

We scanned the glass case and snatched up the last bottle of precious SPF. I asked the shopkeeper, “Do you know where I can find wine here, po?” (The Tagalog word po is a sign of respect.)

“White or red?” he said, to which I countered, “Sugarcane or coconut, please.” He pointed me to the back of his shop, and I squeezed between the shelves of rum, gin, mojito mix … wine!

The front of the bottle featured a red label with a muscular man lifting a tiger and the brand name, Ursus Wine, in bold letters. And in the corner of the label: Made in the Philippines. This must be it. A man wiped down the dusty bottle before taking our cash.

But my sense of triumph wouldn’t last long. I noticed a passerby recoil at the sight of my purchase. Upon further investigation, it was determined to be a Chinese-style herbal wine. The search continued.

Alonso wasn’t surprised at the hurdles I faced as a tourist in hot pursuit of Filipino wines. Visitors are typically offered French wine or American whiskey, not tubâ, a coconut wine, and other island offerings. He said that’s based on a widespread cultural misbelief that Filipino wines aren’t up to snuff. This thinking is a product of the aftershock of colonization. Spain, the U.S., and Japan each took turns occupying the Philippines, which finally gained independence in 1946.

Alonso confided that he only discovered some local drinks later in life. The first time he drank tapuey was at his aunt’s 50th wedding anniversary in 2011. Even as a local, “we didn’t know that we had so many Filipino spirits,” he said.

My quest resumed on the streets of El Nido. Young students on mopeds zoomed to school, and workers corralled sightseers onto beaches for boat tours. As we wandered past one of the many nondescript shops, rows of liquor bottles caught my eye.

After a furtive glance at the shelves, I resigned myself to another defeat when I did a double take: three boxes of Vigan Basi sugarcane wine tucked in the top corner. They cost 500 pisos, or about $9—jackpot.

Back at the bungalow, I let the bottle chill in the mini fridge for about an hour before pouring the cognac-brown wine into a glass. The aroma was potently sweet like that of its distilled cousin, rum. The flavor was strong and tangy, with smooth, earthy undertones. With each passing minute, it grew on me. It was only one variation of local wine, but it tasted like success.

For the rest of the vacation, I resigned myself to the same old cocktails slung by bartenders near and far. Filipino wines largely remain my white whale, swimming in the waters of the South China Sea. Maybe, one day, my thirst will be quenched.

title: Italian Wine Has a Secret Weapon (Hint: It’s Italy)
summary:
At Wine Enthusiast's third-annual Sip of Italy, experts discussed the passion, terroir, and indigenous varieties that makes Italian wine so unique.

The post Italian Wine Has a Secret Weapon (Hint: It’s Italy) appeared first on Wine Enthusiast.
content:
Italian wine hardly needs a sales pitch. But like everywhere in the wine world, Italian pros are grappling with how best to set the industry up for success amid changing consumer tastes, a warming climate, and a tumultuous economic landscape—all while enjoying what we love about Italian wine in the first place.

“Italy is a state of mind. That’s the secret,” says Salvatore Napolitano, executive managing director of Terlato‘s Italian portfolio. At the end of the day, he argues, we need to remember what Italian culture represents—“conviviality, sharing, engaging people of different backgrounds and sensibilities”—because “wine is a conduit for it.” 

On September 14 at City Winery in New York City, Wine Enthusiast held its third-annual Sip of Italy event. With a trade portion that featured a panel of Italian wine experts, as well as a walkaround tasting with bottles from over 100 producers poured, the event was a lively summit on the future of Italy’s dynamic wine scene. 

Here’s what we took away from it.

Let Italy be Italy.

WE Writer-at-Large Jeff Porter opened the panel by acknowledging that, more than anything else, Italian wine stands for “passion” and “conviviality.” This theme came up repeatedly, both in the trade panel and on the tasting floor, as pros court a new generation of drinkers who are less impressed with pedigree and more drawn to experiences.

Napolitano argues that the country’s lack of a cohesive, singular voice, due to its relatively recent unification, is part of what makes the wine scene so special and “democratic.” The other part is the land—and the special relationship Italians have with it.

“Geologically speaking, we have one of the most unique terroirs in the world,” he says. “We are great farmers because we speak to the land.” 

As Michael Duffy, sommelier and wine director at Daniel Humm’s forthcoming restaurant, Humm, puts it: “Italy needs to let itself be Italy.” Wine professionals should remember that, in Italy, “wine is food,” he says. “Whether the wine you’re drinking is a $20 Gaglioppo or a storied bottle from the cellar that’s worth thousands.”

‘Less-famous’ regions are the future.

Duffy predicts that the lesser-known Italian wine regions—Alto Adige, Valle d’Aosta, Southern Italy—are “the new frontier.”

“Due to several factors, climate change being an inevitable factor… we’re going to have to start looking to new-to-some places where great wines are going to be grown and made,” he says.  

The same is true for grape varietals. Italy is a land of countless indigenous grapes, most of which are largely unknown to international consumers. That doesn’t mean the consumer isn’t interested. When Duffy was the wine director at New York’s acclaimed Italian restaurant Rezdora, he decided not to pour international varieties by the glass. “We can’t just respond to the market,” he says. “We have to create the market where [it doesn’t] exist.”

Italian food is made for Italian wine.

That seems like a simple sentiment, but it may be the key to telling the story of just how spectacular Italian wine really is.

Michael Laudenslager, a Wine Enthusiast Writer-at-Large who reviews wines from Tuscany, Southern Italy, and Sardinia, thinks that the key to marketing lesser-known Italian wines, both in retail and at restaurants, is to highlight the foods made in those same regions. Think Ligurian wines and pesto, Campanian wines and Bufala mozzarella, etc.

“There should be a shift towards wine as a part of everyday life, like it’s food,” says Valerie Pimpinelli, general manager and buyer for Flatiron Wines & Spirits. “Taking the pretension out is the number one thing.”

The consumer isn’t stupid.

For the industry to succeed, wine needs to feel more accessible and less intimidating. But that shouldn’t come at the expense of detailed storytelling.

“A cultural trend we should all fight is the TL:DR-ification of everything,” says Duffy. “It’s this idea that people don’t want to engage with a serious book or a long story. That’s thinking the consumer is stupid.”

That doesn’t mean, however, that they necessarily want to hear about hyper-technical production methods of wine when they’re choosing a bottle at the store. “People don’t care about the pH or size of barrels,” says Pimpinelli frankly. “It almost diminishes the pleasure.”

Bottled wine cocktails are hot.

On the tasting floor, product innovation was on full display, as many producers lean into consumer taste for wine cocktails. Brightly colored bottles of ready-to-drink mimosas, bellinis, and spritzes littered the tables, while trays of mimosas floated around the room.

These drinks tend to be much lower in abv than regular wine, typically hovering around 4 to 7%, which makes them attractive to the growing contingent of drinkers searching for lower-proof options. They also lean on the sweeter side, making them an ideal choice for an aperitif.

In Italy, “aperitivo is part of the culture,” says Porter. “Now, producers are making it even more accessible by having them in the RTDs. We’ve seen that in the grocery stores in Italy, and now we’re seeing it more here.”

The Canella Family, pioneers of RTD wine cocktails who have been making their bottled bellinis since 1988, have recently begun making a special bottling specifically for Costco’s Kirkland brand. Alvise Canella, the third-generation Canella who works alongside his brother to oversee production, believes their success can be partly attributed to the simple ingredients in their products. They contain no added sugars, relying on the fruits’ natural sugars instead, and they opt to preserve through pasteurization as opposed to using dangerous additives.

Elsewhere in the tasting room, importers showed off a classic limoncello spritz and Casa Cipriani’s beloved bellini in RTD form. They spoke of success across the United States and abroad, and they hinted at smaller formats (187 mls) making a splash in the future.

title: This Summer-to-Fall Vegetable Dish Is Straight Out of the South of France
summary:
If you’re overwhelmed by the abundance of zucchinis and tomatoes this time of year, make Tian Provençal.

The post This Summer-to-Fall Vegetable Dish Is Straight Out of the South of France appeared first on Wine Enthusiast.
content:
The end of summer is always a little bittersweet. But the cooler weather paired with the last burst of summer produce is a sweet spot worth celebrating. 

Cookbook author and master entertainer Chloe Crane-Leroux’s Tian Provençal makes the most of the season. Similar to ratatouille, but made with a slightly different technique, thinly sliced zucchini, eggplant, and tomatoes are paired with a robust sauce of roasted red peppers, tomatoes, and fresh herbs. It is then baked in the oven until the sauce is bubbly and the vegetables are lightly caramelized—making the most of bright, seasonal flavors without killing your AC bill at the height of peak summer heat.

It’s also downright beautiful, which is why Crane-Leroux loves serving it to guests. It feeds a crowd and seamlessly pairs with a wide variety of starters and sides, and she says, “it is really the perfect transition meal from summer to fall.”

How Chloé Crane-Leroux Sweeps Dinner Guests Away to Provence

If you can’t go all the way to France, hosting a Provençal-style soiree is the next best thing. Here’s how the cookbook author and photographer pulls it off.

Read More

Tian Provençal

Courtesy of Chloe Crane-Leroux

Ingredients

2 medium zucchinis, thinly sliced
2 medium eggplants, thinly sliced
3 large ripe tomatoes, thinly sliced
1 medium red onion, roughly chopped
2 garlic cloves, minced
1 red bell pepper
2 tablespoons extra virgin olive oil
1 (14 ounce) can diced tomatoes
1 teaspoon fresh thyme leaves
1 teaspoon fresh rosemary, finely chopped
½ teaspoon sea salt
½ teaspoon freshly ground black pepper
1 handful fresh basil, roughly torn

Directions

Preheat your grill to high. Place the red bell pepper directly on the grill grates. Char it, turning occasionally, until the skin is blackened and blistered, for 8 to 10 minutes.

Remove from the grill, place in a bowl, and cover with a lid or plastic wrap for 10 minutes to steam. Peel off the charred skin, remove the seeds, and roughly chop the flesh.

Preheat your oven to 375°F (190°C). Thinly slice the zucchini, eggplant, and tomatoes into uniform rounds, about ¼ inch thick. Set aside.

Heat the olive oil in a large oven-safe pan or skillet over medium heat. Add the minced garlic and roughly chopped red onion. Sauté for 2 to 3 minutes, stirring occasionally, until the onion is soft and fragrant.

Stir in the canned diced tomatoes, grilled bell pepper, fresh thyme, rosemary, salt, and pepper. Let the mixture simmer for 5 minutes, then spread it evenly across the bottom of the pan.

Arrange the zucchini, eggplant, and tomato slices following the form of your baking dish (mine is round) on top of the tomato-onion base, alternating them to create a colorful pattern. Slightly overlap the slices for a visually appealing presentation.

Drizzle the layered vegetables with a little extra olive oil.

Sprinkle lightly with salt and pepper.

Cover the pan loosely with foil and bake for 30 minutes.

Remove the foil and bake for an additional 20 to 30 minutes, or until the vegetables are tender and slightly caramelized.

Remove from the oven and let it cool. Sprinkle basil and serve.

title: How Chloé Crane-Leroux Sweeps Dinner Guests Away to Provence
summary:
If you can’t go all the way to France, hosting a Provençal-style soiree is the next best thing. Here’s how the cookbook author and photographer pulls it off.

The post How Chloé Crane-Leroux Sweeps Dinner Guests Away to Provence appeared first on Wine Enthusiast.
content:
On her first trip to Provence in 2023, visual artist and cookbook author Chloé Crane-Leroux felt like her heart was “cracked open.” During the trip, she was drawn to the region in a way she had never experienced before. “I was like ‘this is where I’m meant to be,’” she says. “I just felt like I belonged there.” 

Since then, Crane-Leroux has been splitting her time between Provence and New York with trips across the sea at least every two months, but her connection to France didn’t come out of nowhere. Throughout her childhood, she visited Paris and other areas of the countryside with her family nearly every year.

Her passion for cooking and entertaining also stems from her parents, who were avid hosts all throughout her childhood. “We just always wanted to have friends over, and that’s exactly what my parents did,” she says. “They had friends over all the time, and I just really, really loved that.” 

As she grew up and went off on her own, Crane-Leroux continued both of those childhood traditions. She regularly hosted friends for plant-based dinners at her New York City apartment and traveled to France. Next spring, she’s bringing fans along for the journey with her first immersive retreat in the heart of Provence at the Hôtel Crillon le Brave.

Over five days, Crane-Leroux will take attendees into her world with trips to local food and antique markets, an olive oil tasting, and hands-on cooking workshops. In anticipation of the retreat, we caught up with the plant-based host extraordinaire to get her inside tips on throwing an unforgettable Provençal-style party—sans meat. Whether you want to celebrate seasonal produce, save money while serving farmers’ market fare, or just level up your hosting game, read on for Crane-Leroux’s tips on being the consummate host.

Open Up with Apéro

“Hosting doesn’t have to be scary,” Crane-Leroux says. “A lot of people get intimidated because they want it to be perfect and they overthink it.” That’s why she insists that the path to becoming a better host starts with small steps.

“My favorite thing is apéro, which is basically a French happy hour,” she says. All you need are some small bites and drinks, which Crane-Leroux says can last the whole evening or can trickle into a full dinner. “It’s the perfect way to start hosting because it’s not a full meal and it doesn’t feel so extravagant.”

Wine is Crane-Leroux’s beverage pairing of choice, especially when looking for ease. “In the summer, I love a glass of crisp rosé, especially if we’re starting with little bites,” she says. Sometimes, in the fall or winter, she’ll gravitate towards a red wine—”they’re a bit cozier”—but she enjoys whites year round. “You can never go wrong with a Sancerre or a Chablis.”

While she rarely enjoys cocktails, Crane-Leroux will sometimes indulge in a wine spritz. If you’re up to the challenge of making it at home, go for her favorite combo: a Lillet spritz with a wedge of grapefruit.

Showcase Fresh, Seasonal Ingredients

Whether you’re focusing on snacks or a sit-down dinner, Crane-Leroux is all about celebrating the seasons—even when it comes to tablescapes and decor. She incorporates seasonal vegetables into the floral arrangements or goes full-on produce-focused, like this whimsical tomato tablescape. The rest of the table setting builds on this rustic approach with mismatched wine glasses and candlesticks of varying heights. Crane-Leroux says that this “adds this kind of coziness that everybody loves at a dinner.”

Crane-Leroux also considers seasonality and visual presentation while planning her menus.

“Going to the farmers’ market and getting inspired by what is out there is the best way to come up with a recipe,” she says. “Honing into these key ingredients and eating in a way that just feels like how the earth intended is so great.”

Obviously, this changes throughout the year. In summer and early fall when the tomatoes and zucchini are still really good, Crane-Leroux likes to serve Tian Provençal. Similar to ratatouille but with a prettier presentation, the traditional dish spotlights fresh produce and looks absolutely gorgeous on the dinner table.

This Summer-to-Fall Vegetable Dish Is Straight Out of the South of France

If you’re overwhelmed by the abundance of zucchinis and tomatoes this time of year, make Tian Provençal.

Read More

Galettes and rustic tarts are another eye-catching way that Crane-Leroux likes to center seasonal produce. They’re endlessly adaptable and deceptively easy, especially considering how impressive they appear.

“Truly, you can put anything on puff pastry, and I think it would be amazing,” she says. In the summertime and early fall, this often manifests as tomato or zucchini galettes, while cooler months lend themselves well to winter squashes.

Wine Picks Should Elevate the Produce

Plant-based food often gets a bad rap for being difficult to pair, but Crane-Leroux insists that couldn’t be farther from the truth.

“Wine comes from the earth and plant-based food comes from the earth,” she says. “The flavors of the wine can be complementary to a specific vegetable,” she says. “So you can really take dishes that have those particular ingredients and tie it back to a certain wine.”

Have you ever tasted a wine that distinctly feels like biting into a tomato? Crane-Leroux has, and she finds that pairing those kinds of wines with a dish featuring farm-fresh heirloom tomatoes beautifully elevates the flavors of each. She also loves pairing an earthy Lambrusco with red sauce pizza or a rich Port with cherry pie.

“A wine that brings those flavors out will also just make the dish even better,” Crane-Leroux says.

Let Guests Handle Dessert—But Add a Signature Touch

When guests inevitably offer to bring something, Crane-Leroux will often concede dessert. 

“It lifts a little bit of weight off of me from cooking,” she says, and it can add a fun element of surprise to the evening if you’re not quite sure what they’re bringing. Even so, she likes to prepare some sort of accompaniment for dessert to add a homemade feeling and an extra special touch. This could take the shape of anything from ice cream or caramel sauce to shaved chocolate or edible flowers to decorate. 

“You didn’t do a full-blown dessert—your guest brought that,” she says, “but then adding that little touch as the host, even just to make the dish prettier, I think that is the best of both worlds.”
